title: String Compression II
statement:
Run-length encoding rewrites a string block by block: every maximal stretch of two or more equal adjacent characters becomes that character followed by the stretch's length in decimal, while a character with no equal neighbour is written alone (no `1` is added). For instance `"zzzyxxxxxxxxxx"` encodes to `"z3yx10"`.

You may remove up to `k` characters, at any positions, from `s`; the remaining characters keep their order and close up. Return the smallest length the encoding of the resulting string can have. Removing every character leaves the empty string, whose encoding has length `0`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every set of at most `k` deletions is exponential. Instead, decide the string from left to right: the character at `i` is either deleted, or it is kept and becomes the first letter of a block. If it starts a block, it is worth absorbing later copies of the same letter into that block by deleting the different letters between them. Once the block ends, the rest of the string is the same kind of problem on a suffix with a smaller budget, so a table over (start index, deletions left) captures everything.

## Approach

1. `encodedLength(count)` is the cost of one block: 1 for a single letter, plus 1, 2 or 3 digits for counts of 2–9, 10–99 or 100.
2. `dp[i][budget]` is the shortest encoding of `s[i..]` using at most `budget` deletions; `dp[n][*] = 0`. Fill `i` from right to left.
3. Option one: delete `s[i]`, giving `dp[i + 1][budget - 1]` when `budget > 0`.
4. Option two: keep `s[i]` and extend its block to each end `j`. Count copies of `s[i]` in `same` and other letters (which must be deleted) in `removed`. Stop once `removed` exceeds `budget`.
5. Each end `j` costs `encodedLength(same) + dp[j + 1][budget - removed]`; keep the minimum. The answer is `dp[0][k]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "aaabcccd"`, `k = 2`. At `i = 7` (`d`), `dp[7][0] = 1` and `dp[7][1] = 0`. For `"cccd"` (`i = 4`) with one deletion, block `ccc` costs 2 and `dp[7][1] = 0`, so `dp[4][1] = 2`. For `"bcccd"` (`i = 3`) with two deletions, deleting `b` gives `dp[4][1] = 2`. Finally at `i = 0`, block `aaa` (`j = 2`, `removed = 0`) costs 2 plus `dp[3][2] = 2`, so `dp[0][2] = 4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · k): each of the n · (k + 1) states scans up to n ends.
- Space: O(n · k) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- A count of 1 adds no digit, but 10 and 100 add two and three digits; `9 → 10` makes a block longer.
- Deleting all of a letter's other characters can merge two blocks, as in `"aabbaa"`; extending a block over deleted letters handles this.
- Without deletions left, `best` must start at `Infinity`, not at a deletion option.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i][budget]` | best encoded length of `s[i..]` with at most `budget` deletions |
| `best` | minimum found for the current state |
| `j` | where the block that starts at `i` ends |
| `same` | copies of `s[i]` kept in that block |
| `removed` | other letters deleted inside that block |

narration.3: A block of count letters costs one character plus the digits of the count when it is above 1.
narration.4: dp[i][budget] will hold the best encoding of s from i onward; the row for i = n stays 0.
narration.6: Solve suffixes from the shortest to the longest so later rows are ready.
narration.7: Try every number of deletions still allowed.
narration.8: Option one: delete s[i] and solve the next suffix with one fewer deletion.
narration.11: Option two: keep s[i] as the start of a block and try each end j.
narration.12: Another copy of the block's letter joins the block...
narration.15: ...while any other letter inside the block must be deleted.
narration.17: Too many deletions are needed; longer blocks only need more.
narration.20: Cost of this block plus the best encoding of everything after it.
narration.22: Store the best choice for this suffix and budget.
narration.25: The whole string with all k deletions available is the answer.
